E2 — Diode Models: Shockley, Piecewise-Linear Models and Multi-Diode Circuits (T2, Weeks 1–2)

Why this matters in the exam: The practice test spends 13 of its 50 marks here. Q2 (5 marks) is a straight calculation with , and Q3 (8 marks) is a three-diode circuit with the third piecewise-linear model: redraw, verify conduction, find . Q1 part II (dynamic resistance as the slope of the I–V curve) adds 1 more mark. The test reuses workshop questions word for word (Q4 is WS3 Q13 and Q5 is WS3 Q12), so WS2 Q8–17 and WS3 Q1–8 and Q15–17 are the most likely sources for the next paper. This block teaches the method: which equation to use, which model to draw, and how to prove each diode’s state.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The Shockley (exponential) model

with J/K and C (both on the test formula sheet). is the reverse saturation current and is the ideality factor. The course uses from 1 to 2.

Two results to remember:

  • Full or approximate equation? At both give the same to four figures (WS2 Q8 i). If they don’t agree, the diode is not fully on.

1.2 Temperature effects (Week 1 slide 50)

Effect Course rule How to use it
Forward characteristic Shifts left by about 2.5 mV per °C rise (Si) At a fixed current,
Reverse current Doubles for every 10 °C rise (WS3 Q2)
Proportional to Recompute at the new temperature. Then rises with too
Breakdown voltage Can rise or fall with temperature Descriptive only

Trap: a hotter diode has a smaller forward drop but a larger leakage current. Don’t let the rising talk you into a larger . The growth of wins.

1.3 The three piecewise-linear models (the course’s names)

The course numbers the models (WS2 Q17, WS3 Q15, practice test Q3 “third piecewise linear model”):

Model Course name ON state (forward, conducting) OFF state ON is valid if OFF is valid if
1st Ideal model Short circuit, Open circuit
2nd Voltage drop model, (constant-voltage drop, “simplified” circuit, 0.7 V for Si) Ideal diode in series with a source (+ on the anode side) Open circuit
3rd Voltage drop with resistor model, (“piecewise-linear equivalent circuit”, plus ) Ideal diode in series with a source and a resistor Open circuit
  • In every model the OFF diode is an open circuit (WS2 Q17 note).
  • The 3rd-model resistor is the average ac resistance, the slope of a chord between two points: (point to point). WS3 Q5 gives Ge as 0.3 V + 4.62 Ω and GaAs as 1.2 V + 4.62 Ω. The formula sheet gives the knee voltages : Ge 0.3 V, Si 0.7 V, GaAs 1.2 V.
  • In the 3rd model the voltage across a conducting diode is , which is more than .

Drop towards 1 V and watch the three model operating points spread apart from the exponential one; at 5 V they nearly agree.

2. The method

Type A: exponential-model numbers (WS2 Q8–10, WS3 Q1, Q4, practice test Q2)

Recognise it: the question says “exponential model”, “Shockley”, gives or , or gives currents of very different sizes (0.1 mA to 10 mA).

  1. Convert to kelvin and compute . Write it to four significant figures.
  2. Decide which of four sub-types it is:
    • , and given, find : .
    • , and given, find : use the full equation .
    • A change in current, find : . No is needed.
    • Two points, find and : divide the two equations to get , then back-substitute one point to get . Check with the other point.
  3. Sanity check: per decade of current.

Type B: temperature (WS3 Q2)

  1. Leakage: . Forward drop: mV/°C at fixed current.
  2. If a resistor carries (reverse-biased diode feeding a resistor), then scales by the same factor.

Type C: resistance levels and building a model (WS3 Q5, Q6)

  1. DC: read one point off the curve and divide.
  2. AC: draw the tangent at the Q-point, or take a small symmetric span either side of it, and compute .
  3. 3rd model: draw the chord between the two given points. , and is where the chord cuts the axis (the course takes the knee value).

Type D: diode circuits, the four-step assume-and-verify method (WS3 Q7, Q8, Q15–17, practice test Q3)

Recognise it: a circuit with one or more diodes and resistors or sources, and an instruction to “find ”, “find the diode currents” or “verify whether … conducting”.

  1. Choose the model. Use the one the question names (ideal, , or ). Write it down.
  2. Guess each diode’s state and write it down. For example “Assume D1 ON, D2 OFF”. If a diode’s anode is nearer the more positive source, guess ON. If its cathode is nearer the more positive point, guess OFF. Look for opposing batteries.
  3. Analyse the linear circuit. Redraw it: ON diodes become their model branch, OFF diodes become open circuits. Solve using KVL, KCL, Thévenin or superposition. Compute exactly what you need to check:
    • for each ON diode, its current in the anode → cathode direction;
    • for each OFF diode, its voltage . An OFF branch carries no current, so its resistors drop nothing.
  4. Verify. ON needs . OFF needs (or for the ideal model). If any check fails, flip that diode (usually the one with the most negative current) and go back to step 3. Repeat until every check passes. Then, and only then, compute .

With diodes there are possible combinations, but a sensible first guess usually needs at most one flip. Write the check out explicitly, for example “ mA , so the assumption fails”. The verification is where the marks are (4 of the 8 in practice test Q3).

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Dropping in . With , two decades are 179 mV, not 119 mV.
  • Wrong . Recompute it from the stated temperature. If the question gives none, say which value you assume (25 mV, 25.9 mV or 26 mV).
  • Confusing with . Static (about 175 Ω in WS3 Q6) is two orders of magnitude bigger than the dynamic slope (a few Ω).
  • Getting the 3rd-model diode voltage wrong. It is , not . In practice test Q3 the chain drops (in kΩ and mA).
  • Treating the model as a free choice. Q3 says the 3rd model with 0.6 V and 0.2 kΩ. If you used 0.7 V per diode, V would exceed the 2 V of headroom and the diodes would come out OFF. The model changes the answer.
  • Not writing down the check, or checking the wrong quantity. ON needs a current check. OFF needs a voltage check. A correct with no verification loses the verification marks.
  • Getting the sign of wrong for an OFF diode. It is always . An OFF branch carries no current, so its resistors drop 0 V but its batteries still count.
  • Temperature direction. falls by 2.5 mV/°C, while doubles every 10 °C. With a 20 °C rise that is a factor of 4, not 2.

Notes where my working differs from the official solutions:

  • WS3 Q4: I get 0.791 mA, and the official answer is 0.789 mA. The difference is rounding in .
  • WS3 Q1: I get 296.06 mV, and the official answer is 296.11 mV. Same reason.

WS2 Q12 (course question). Do you expect a linear relationship between voltage and current in the two circuits below? Why? Discuss it in your group.

Solution

Yes, both are linear. Each contains only linear elements (a resistor and an independent source), so by superposition the terminal – relation is a straight line. Here is an independent current source, not a diode’s saturation current.

WS2 Q14 (course question). In the Fig. 5, full diode operational regions are shown according to the current direction and voltage polarities in the figure. Identify the regions and voltages mentioned in the figure. Discuss the diode’s operation in each region in your group.

Solution
  • Region A: breakdown. Region B: reverse bias (only flows). Region C: partial conduction. Region D: full conduction.
  • Voltage A: Zener knee / breakdown voltage. Voltage B: cut-in voltage. Voltage C: forward voltage drop.

WS2 Q15 (course question). Considering the diode’s operational regions in Question 14, we can linearize the diode’s operation using the piece-wise linearization technique. How many pieces do you think we need? Discuss it in your group. Note: Piecewise linear curve is a connected sequence of line segments. Piecewise linear function is a function whose domain can be decomposed into pieces on which the function is linear.

Solution

Four linear pieces, one per region (breakdown, reverse, partial conduction, full conduction), because each region behaves differently and no single straight line fits two of them.

WS2 Q16 (course question). In the circuit shown below, an ideal diode is connected to a multimeter. The device shows 35.733 MΩ. How do you explain this value? Is there anything wrong with the diode or our circuit? What do you expect to see if we rotate the diode connection? Discuss it in your group.

Solution

The ohmmeter’s own source is reverse biasing the diode, so it reads the very large reverse resistance (almost an open circuit). Nothing is wrong. Rotate the diode and it is forward biased, so you expect a very low reading (a few to a few tens of ohms). This is a quick way to find a diode’s polarity, but the forward reading is at one unknown operating point, so it is not the diode’s forward resistance .

3. : each diode becomes in series with (that is, ).

In reverse bias every piecewise-linear model is just an open circuit.
